source.text: Thousand Hands Sutra, a traditional Korean Buddhist ritual text. Its central dhāraṇī is from Bhagavaddharma, trans., Sutra of the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī of the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara (Taishō T1060)
source.license: Original text and arrangement: traditional ritual text, public domain
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

c01.heading: Mantra for Purifying Speech
c01.meaning: Auspicious, auspicious, greatly auspicious, supremely auspicious, svāhā
c01.commentary: Before chanting begins, this mantra purifies the mouth. It carries the resolve to cleanse a mouth soiled by harsh words and lies before reading the sutra.
c01.plain: The mantra for purifying the karma of speech. Following tradition, it is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c02.heading: Mantra for Comforting the Spirits of the Five Directions
c02.meaning: I take refuge in all the Buddhas everywhere. Oṃ, dhuru dhuru devī svāhā
c02.commentary: This mantra brings peace to every being dwelling east, west, south, north and center, inside and out, around the place of chanting. It quiets the surroundings as the ceremony begins.
c02.plain: The mantra for comforting all the spirits within and beyond the five directions. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c03.heading: Verse for Opening the Sutra
c03.plain: The supreme, profound and subtle Dharma is hard to meet even in a hundred thousand million kalpas. Now that I can see, hear, receive and keep it, may I understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
c03.commentary: A verse recited before opening a sutra. It recalls how rare a chance it is to meet the Buddha's teaching, and resolves to grasp its true meaning rather than just read the words. It opens the chanting of many sutras, not only this one.

c04.heading: Mantra for Opening the Dharma Treasury
c04.commentary: This mantra opens the door of the storehouse that holds the teachings. With the mind settled by the opening verse, it leads into the chanting proper.
c04.plain: The mantra for opening the treasury of the Dharma. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c05.heading: Invocation of the Great Dhāraṇī (1)
c05.plain: I invoke the vast, perfect, unhindered Great Compassion Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of the thousand hands and thousand eyes. I bow my head to Avalokiteśvara, lord of great compassion. Your vows are vast and deep, your form is perfect; adorned with a thousand arms, you protect everyone, and with the light of a thousand eyes you watch over the whole world. Within true words you speak secret words; within a mind free of contrivance you give rise to compassion. You swiftly fulfill all wishes and forever wipe away all karmic wrongs.
c05.commentary: Before chanting the Great Dhāraṇī, this part praises Avalokiteśvara and requests the dhāraṇī. The thousand hands stand for help that reaches everywhere; the thousand eyes for care that misses no suffering. The "secret words" are the dhāraṇī that follows.

c06.heading: Invocation of the Great Dhāraṇī (2)
c06.plain: Heavenly beings, dragons and holy ones all protect with compassion, and a hundred thousand samādhis are cultivated at once. The body that holds this dhāraṇī becomes a banner of light; the mind that holds it becomes a treasury of spiritual power. May I wash away the dust of affliction, cross the sea of suffering, and at once reach the gate of skillful means to awakening. Now I chant it and vow to take refuge; may all my wishes be fulfilled as my heart intends.
c06.commentary: This part speaks of the merit of holding the dhāraṇī, and the chanter vows to take refuge. It sings that holding the dhāraṇī makes the body like a banner lighting the darkness, and the mind like a storehouse full of wisdom and strength.

c07.heading: The Ten Vows
c07.plain: Taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara of great compassion, I vow: may I swiftly know all dharmas; may I soon gain the eye of wisdom; may I swiftly save all beings; may I soon gain good skillful means; may I swiftly board the ship of prajñā; may I soon cross the sea of suffering; may I swiftly attain the path of precepts, meditation and wisdom; may I soon climb the mountain of nirvana; may I swiftly enter the house of non-doing; may I soon become one with the Dharma-nature body.
c07.commentary: Ten vows offered to Avalokiteśvara. They move from knowing (knowing the Dharma, the eye of wisdom) through action (saving beings, skillful means) and practice (prajñā, the three trainings) to final awakening (nirvana, the Dharma-nature body). "Swiftly" and "soon" alternate, adding urgency.

c08.heading: The Six Directions
c08.plain: If I go toward the mountain of knives, may it break apart by itself; if I go toward the boiling cauldron, may it die down by itself; if I go toward the hells, may they dry up by themselves; if I go toward the hungry ghosts, may they be filled by themselves; if I go toward the asuras, may their evil minds be tamed by themselves; if I go toward the animals, may they gain great wisdom by themselves.
c08.commentary: A vow that wherever one goes among the worlds of pain, the suffering there will vanish. It expresses the bodhisattva's heart: not seeking one's own comfort, but going to the most painful places to end the pain there.

c09.heading: Names of the Bodhisattvas
c09.plain: I take refuge in Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Thousand-Handed, Cintāmaṇicakra, the Great Wheel, Avalokiteśvara the Free, Right Approach, Full Moon, Water Moon, Kuṇḍalī, the Eleven-Faced, and all the great bodhisattvas. I take refuge in our original teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
c09.commentary: Chanters call the names of Avalokiteśvara's many forms and the bodhisattvas who accompany him, and take refuge. The Thousand-Handed, Cintāmaṇicakra, the Eleven-Faced and others are forms Avalokiteśvara takes to meet different beings. Finally they take refuge in Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara's teacher, calling his name three times.

c10.heading: The Great Dhāraṇī of Wondrous Phrases
c10.commentary: The central dhāraṇī of the Thousand Hands Sutra, often called the Great Compassion Mantra. It comes from the Sutra of the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī of the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara, and is read with the pronunciation handed down in Korea. It opens with refuge in the Three Jewels and Avalokiteśvara, then praises Avalokiteśvara's many forms (such as Nīlakaṇṭha) and prays that obstacles vanish and awakening is realized. It is traditionally chanted three times.
c10.plain: A dhāraṇī that takes refuge in Avalokiteśvara, praises his great compassion and virtue, and asks that all afflictions and obstacles fall away. Following tradition, it is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c11.heading: Praise of the Four Directions
c11.plain: First, sprinkling the east, the practice place is cleansed; second, sprinkling the south, coolness is gained; third, sprinkling the west, the Pure Land is complete; fourth, sprinkling the north, there is lasting peace.
c11.commentary: This sings of sprinkling water blessed by the dhāraṇī in four directions to purify the practice place. Even without real water, it can be taken to mean that a mind purified by the dhāraṇī cleanses its surroundings.

c12.heading: Praise of the Practice Place
c12.plain: The practice place is pure, without a speck of dust, and the Three Jewels, heavenly beings and dragons descend here. Now I hold and chant the wondrous mantra; may you grant your compassion and protect me unseen.
c12.commentary: A verse inviting the Three Jewels and guardian spirits into the place purified by the previous praise. It also prepares for the repentance that follows.

c13.heading: Verse of Repentance
c13.plain: All the harmful karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, anger and delusion, born of body, speech and mind. I now repent of it all.
c13.commentary: A repentance verse from the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Practices and Vows in the Avataṃsaka Sutra. It names the root of wrongdoing as the three poisons of greed, anger and delusion, and the channels through which they show as body, speech and mind. Repentance begins by blaming no one else and admitting what one has done.

c14.heading: The Twelve Buddhas Who Remove Karmic Obstacles
c14.plain: I take refuge in the twelve Buddhas who remove karmic obstacles through repentance: Jewel-Victory Treasury Buddha, Jewel-Light King Blazing Fire Buddha, All Incense and Flowers Sovereign Power King Buddha, Hundred Billion Ganges Sands Certainty Buddha, Majestic Virtue Buddha, Diamond-Firm Subduing and Scattering Buddha, Universal Light Moon Palace Wondrous Sound Honored King Buddha, Joyful Treasury Maṇi Jewel Heap Buddha, Inexhaustible Incense Victorious King Buddha, Lion Moon Buddha, Joyful Adornment Pearl King Buddha, and Indra's Jewel Banner Maṇi Victorious Light Buddha.
c14.commentary: This calls the names of twelve Buddhas who melt away karmic obstacles through repentance. Each name holds a symbol such as jewels, light, incense, diamond or lion, inviting us to picture a mind made bright and strong by repentance.

c15.heading: Repentance of the Ten Evils
c15.plain: Today I repent of the grave wrongs of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, idle talk, divisive speech, harsh speech, greed, anger and delusion.
c15.commentary: Repentance for the ten harmful acts, one by one. They divide into three of body (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), four of speech (lying, idle talk, divisive speech, harsh speech) and three of mind (greed, anger, delusion). Notice that speech accounts for the most.

c16.heading: Verses of Repentance
c16.plain: Wrongs piled up over a hundred kalpas are swept away in a single thought, like fire burning dry grass until nothing is left. Wrongdoing has no nature of its own; it arises from the mind. When the mind falls away, the wrong falls away too. When both the wrong and the mind are gone and both are empty, this is called true repentance.
c16.commentary: Two verses that reveal the deeper meaning of repentance. The first speaks of the power of a single sincere thought; the second of emptiness: even wrongdoing has no fixed substance. True repentance is not staying bound by guilt, but seeing clearly the mind that gave rise to the wrong and letting it go.

c17.heading: Mantra of Repentance
c17.meaning: I take refuge in all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, svāhā
c17.commentary: This mantra seals the repentance above, affirming that one has repented before all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
c17.plain: The mantra that completes repentance. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c18.heading: Praise of Cundī
c18.plain: This mantra is the gathered merit of Cundī Bodhisattva. Whoever chants it constantly with a quiet mind cannot be harmed by any great calamity. In heaven and among humans they will receive blessings equal to a Buddha's; whoever meets this wish-fulfilling jewel will surely attain unequalled awakening. I take refuge in Great Cundī Bodhisattva, mother of seven koṭis of Buddhas.
c18.commentary: A verse praising Cundī Bodhisattva and the merit of her mantra, likened to a wish-fulfilling jewel that grants anything. "Mother of seven koṭis of Buddhas" means mother of seventy million Buddhas, showing that Cundī symbolizes the wisdom from which countless Buddhas are born.

c19.heading: Mantra for Purifying the Dharma Realm
c19.commentary: A one-syllable mantra that purifies the whole world around the chanter. It has been handed down together with the Cundī mantra as its preparation.
c19.plain: The mantra for purifying the whole Dharma realm. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c20.heading: Mantra for Protecting the Body
c20.commentary: A mantra that protects the practitioner's body. After purifying the Dharma realm, one protects oneself, then moves on to the main mantra.
c20.plain: The mantra for protecting the body. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c21.heading: Avalokiteśvara's Six-Syllable Great Bright King Mantra
c21.meaning: Oṃ, jewel in the lotus, hūṃ (a common interpretation)
c21.commentary: Often called the Six-Syllable Mantra, this is Avalokiteśvara's best-known mantra and one of the most widely chanted across the Buddhist world, Tibet included. Maṇi means jewel and padme lotus; together they are read as compassion and wisdom that stay unstained even in the mud.
c21.plain: The six-syllable mantra holding the original mind of Avalokiteśvara. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c22.heading: Cundī Mantra
c22.meaning: I take refuge in the seventy million fully awakened Buddhas. Thus it is said: oṃ cale cule cundī svāhā (a common interpretation)
c22.commentary: This is the very mantra praised above. The first part takes refuge in seventy million Buddhas; after "tadyathā" (thus it is said) comes the mantra itself.
c22.plain: The mantra of Cundī Bodhisattva. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

c23.heading: Cundī Aspiration
c23.plain: Now I hold and chant the Great Cundī mantra and at once raise the vast vow of awakening. May my meditation and wisdom swiftly become perfectly clear; may all my merits be fulfilled; may excellent blessings adorn everything; and may I attain the Buddha way together with all beings.
c23.commentary: The merit of chanting the mantra flows into aspiration. The spirit of Mahāyāna shows in the last line, which wishes to reach the Buddha way "together with all beings," not alone.

c24.heading: The Tathāgata's Ten Great Vows
c24.plain: May I forever leave the three evil paths; may I swiftly cut off greed, anger and delusion; may I always hear of the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha; may I diligently cultivate precepts, meditation and wisdom; may I always follow and learn from the Buddhas; may I never turn back from the mind of awakening; may I surely be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss; may I swiftly see Amitābha; may I divide my body and appear throughout countless worlds; may I save all beings far and wide.
c24.commentary: Ten aspirations modeled on the vows of the Buddhas. Starting with escaping the evil paths, they pass through practice and rebirth in the Pure Land, and end by saving all beings. Paired with the Ten Vows earlier, they frame the Thousand Hands Sutra with vows at its beginning and end.

c25.heading: The Four Great Vows
c25.plain: Beings are numberless; I vow to save them all. Afflictions are endless; I vow to cut them all. Dharma gates are countless; I vow to learn them all. The Buddha way is supreme; I vow to attain it. I vow to save the beings of my own nature, cut the afflictions of my own nature, learn the Dharma gates of my own nature, and attain the Buddha way of my own nature.
c25.commentary: The four great vows shared by all bodhisattvas. The first four lines face the world outside; the last four turn the same vows inward to one's own nature, the mind. They carry the Seon (Zen) view that beings and afflictions alike come from one's own mind.

c26.heading: Having Vowed, I Take Refuge in the Three Jewels
c26.commentary: With all vows made, the sutra ends by taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha who ever dwell in the ten directions, the whole universe. It begins by purifying the mouth, passes through repentance and vows, and ends by returning to the Three Jewels.
c26.plain: Having made our vows, we offer our lives in homage to the Three Jewels. We take refuge in the Buddhas ever present in the ten directions. We take refuge in the Dharma ever present in the ten directions. We take refuge in the Sangha ever present in the ten directions.

mantra.definition: True words. Sacred words holding the awakening and vows of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, traditionally chanted for their sound rather than translated.

dharani.definition: Means "holding everything." A longer mantra that holds the teaching and its merit. The Great Dhāraṇī of this sutra is the best-known example.

avalokitesvara.definition: The bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world: the bodhisattva of compassion who rescues suffering beings as soon as they call. Also called Gwanjajae, "the one who observes freely."

kalpa.definition: An immeasurably long span of time. A hundred thousand million kalpas means, in effect, an endless time.

tathagata.definition: "Thus come": one who comes from truth. A title of the Buddha.

samadhi.definition: A still, unwavering state of mind gathered in one place.

bodhi.definition: Awakening. Bodhicitta is the resolve to awaken in order to save all beings.

prajnaparamita.definition: Wisdom that sees through to the true nature of things. "The ship of prajñā" likens it to a boat that carries us across the sea of suffering.

three-trainings.definition: The three pillars of practice: precepts (right conduct), meditation (gathering the mind) and wisdom.

nirvana.definition: The stillness in which the fire of affliction has gone out. The "mountain of nirvana" in this sutra likens it to a mountain.

six-realms.definition: The six worlds beings are born into according to karma: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans and heavenly beings. The Six Directions verse is a vow toward the painful ones.

namo.definition: "I take refuge," relying on with body and mind. The same namo as in "Namo Amitābha Buddha."

amitabha.definition: The Buddha of boundless light and life, Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Bliss and teacher of Avalokiteśvara.

bodhimanda.definition: Where practice and ceremonies are held. Originally the spot where the Buddha attained awakening.

pure-land.definition: A pure world where a Buddha dwells, especially Amitābha's Land of Bliss, also called the Land of Peace and Nourishment.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).

three-poisons.definition: The three poisons that harm the mind: greed, anger and delusion.

karma.definition: Actions of body, speech and mind and the force they leave behind. Karmic obstacles are harmful karma that blocks practice.

repentance.definition: Regretting wrongs done and resolving not to repeat them. Traditionally the first character is said to regret past faults, the second future ones.

ten-evils.definition: Ten harmful acts: three of body (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), four of speech (lying, idle talk, divisive speech, harsh speech) and three of mind (greed, anger, delusion).

cundi.definition: A bodhisattva of purity, called "mother of seven koṭis of Buddhas." In Korea she is sometimes seen as a form of Avalokiteśvara.

three-evil-paths.definition: The three most painful worlds: hells, hungry ghosts and animals.

sunyata.definition: Because everything arises in dependence on conditions, nothing has an independent, fixed self. It underlies the repentance verse saying even wrongdoing has no fixed substance.

four-vows.definition: The four great vows of every bodhisattva: to save beings, cut afflictions, learn the Dharma gates and attain the Buddha way.
